exercises.title: Back substitution 3×3
exercises.description: Solve $Rx = y$ with $R = \begin{pmatrix}2&1&-1\\0&3&2\\0&0&4\end{pmatrix}$ and $y = (-1, 1, 8)^T$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$R$ is upper triangular: solve from bottom to top.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
Always start with the last equation: it contains only one unknown.

exercises.title: Forward substitution 3×3
exercises.description: Solve $Ly = b$ with $L = \begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\2&1&0\\-1&3&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $b = (1, 5, 10)^T$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$L$ is lower triangular: solve top to bottom.

Step 2: Substituting
$y_1 = 1$. $y_2 = 5 - 2\cdot 1 = 3$. $y_3 = 10 + 1\cdot 1 - 3\cdot 3 = 2$.

Step 3: Check
Row 3: $-1\cdot 1 + 3\cdot 3 + 2 = 10$ ✓. $y = (1, 3, 2)^T$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
In forward substitution the diagonal entries of $L$ equal $1$ – no division needed.

exercises.title: LU decomposition 2×2
exercises.description: Find the LU decomposition of $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&4\\6&16\end{pmatrix}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
One elimination step: factor $l_{21} = a_{21}/a_{11}$.

Step 3: Result
$L = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$, $R = \begin{pmatrix}2&4\\0&4\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 4: Check
$LR$: row 2: $3\cdot(2,4) + 1\cdot(0,4) = (6, 16)$ ✓.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
$L$ holds the factors (positive), $R$ the eliminated matrix.

exercises.title: Reading off elimination factors
exercises.description: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}3&1&2\\6&5&1\\-3&4&2\end{pmatrix}$: determine $l_{21}, l_{31}$ and the matrix after the first elimination step.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$l_{i1} = a_{i1}/a_{11}$ and row $i$ $-\,l_{i1}\cdot$row 1.

Step 4: Result
$\begin{pmatrix}3&1&2\\0&3&-3\\0&5&4\end{pmatrix}$. The next factor would be $l_{32} = 5/3$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Negative entries below the pivot give negative factors – watch the signs closely.

exercises.title: Solving with given L and R
exercises.description: Let $A = LU$ with $L = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$, $U = \begin{pmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$. Solve $Ax = b$ for $b = (4, 10)^T$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Two triangular systems: $Ly = b$, then $Ux = y$.

Step 2: Forward
$y_1 = 4$, $y_2 = 10 - 2\cdot 4 = 2$.

Step 4: Check
$A = LU = \begin{pmatrix}3&1\\6&4\end{pmatrix}$; $A(1,1)^T = (4, 10)^T$ ✓.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Checking with the original matrix $A$ reveals mistakes in both steps.

exercises.title: Determinant from R
exercises.description: We have $A = LU$ with $L = \begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\2&1&0\\-1&3&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $U = \begin{pmatrix}3&1&2\\0&-2&1\\0&0&5\end{pmatrix}$. Compute $\det A$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$\det A = \det L\cdot\det U$; for triangular matrices: product of the diagonal.

Step 2: Computation
$\det L = 1$, $\det U = 3\cdot(-2)\cdot 5 = -30$. So $\det A = -30$.

Step 3: Takeaway: What matters
Determinant = product of the pivots (with the sign of the row swaps).

exercises.title: Flops of back substitution
exercises.description: Count the operations (multiplications, additions/subtractions, divisions) for back substitution with $n = 3$ and in general.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Row $i$ needs $n - i$ multiplications, $n - i$ subtractions and $1$ division.

Step 3: In general
$\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(2(n-i) + 1\bigr) = n(n-1) + n = n^2$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
Triangular systems cost $n^2$, i.e. $O(n^2)$ – an order of magnitude below the decomposition ($n^3$).

exercises.title: Is Cholesky possible?
exercises.description: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$, $B = \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $C = \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ decide whether a Cholesky decomposition exists.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Requirement: symmetric and positive definite (all leading minors $> 0$).

Step 2: A
Symmetric. Minors: $4 > 0$, $\det = 12 - 4 = 8 > 0$. So spd – Cholesky exists. $l_{11} = 2$, $l_{21} = 1$, $l_{22} = \sqrt{3 - 1} = \sqrt 2$.

Step 3: B and C
$B$: symmetric, but $\det = 1 - 4 = -3 < 0$ – not positive definite (the square root would be of $1 - 4 = -3$). $C$: not symmetric.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
Cholesky needs symmetry AND positive definiteness. A positive diagonal alone is not enough.

exercises.title: 3×3 LU decomposition and solving
exercises.description: Compute the LU decomposition of $A = \begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&5&7\\3&8&14\end{pmatrix}$ and solve $Ax = b$ for $b = (6, 14, 25)^T$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Two elimination steps, then two triangular systems.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Checking $LU = A$ before solving saves error hunting.

exercises.title: LU with partial pivoting
exercises.description: Determine $PA = LU$ for $A = \begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\\7&8&10\end{pmatrix}$ and use it to solve $Ax = b$ with $b = (6, 15, 25)^T$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
In each column swap the entry of largest magnitude to the top as pivot.

Step 2: Step 1
Column 1: $7$ is largest – swap row 3 to the top: $PA$ has rows $(7,8,10), (1,2,3), (4,5,6)$. Factors $\frac17$ and $\frac47$.

Step 4: Step 2
Column 2: $\tfrac67 > \tfrac37$, no swap. $l_{32} = \tfrac12$. $r_{33} = \tfrac27 - \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{11}{7} = -\tfrac12$.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
All factors satisfy $|l_{ik}| \le 1$. Do not forget: $b$ is permuted with $P$.

exercises.title: Cholesky 3×3
exercises.description: Find the Cholesky decomposition of $A = \begin{pmatrix}4&2&2\\2&5&3\\2&3&6\end{pmatrix}$ and solve $Ax = b$ for $b = (8, 10, 11)^T$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Column by column: $l_{jj} = \sqrt{a_{jj} - \sum l_{jk}^2}$, $l_{ij} = (a_{ij} - \sum l_{ik}l_{jk})/l_{jj}$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
All radicands were positive and $L$ is integer – the matrix was spd.

exercises.title: Several right-hand sides
exercises.description: Decompose $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\4&5\end{pmatrix}$ once and use it to solve $Ax = b_1$ and $Ax = b_2$ with $b_1 = (3, 9)^T$, $b_2 = (1, -1)^T$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The decomposition depends only on $A$ – it is reused.

Step 2: Decomposition
$l_{21} = 2$, $r_{22} = 5 - 2\cdot 1 = 3$. $L = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$, $U = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Each further right-hand side costs only $2n^2$ instead of $\frac23 n^3$ flops.

exercises.title: Cost: decomposition vs. inverse
exercises.description: For $n = 1000$ compare the cost of (a) solving with an LU decomposition, (b) computing $A^{-1}$ through $n$ solves and then $x = A^{-1}b$. How much more expensive is (b)?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Decomposition $\tfrac23 n^3$, one solve $2n^2$, matrix-vector product $2n^2$.

Step 2: (a)
$\tfrac23\cdot 10^9 + 2\cdot 10^6 \approx 6.7\cdot 10^{8}$ flops.

Step 3: (b)
Decomposition $\tfrac23 n^3$ plus $n$ solves of $2n^2$ each: $\tfrac23 n^3 + 2n^3 = \tfrac83 n^3 \approx 2.7\cdot 10^{9}$, plus $2n^2$ for $A^{-1}b$.

Step 4: Comparison
Ratio $\approx 4$: the inverse is four times as expensive – and less accurate.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Never compute $A^{-1}$ if you only need $A^{-1}b$.

exercises.title: Pivot example in a 3-digit system
exercises.description: Solve $\begin{pmatrix}0.0001&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}x = \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ in $3$-digit arithmetic (a) without, (b) with a row swap. The exact solution is $x \approx (1.0001,\ 0.9999)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Round to $3$ significant digits after every operation.

Step 5: Backward (b)
$x_2 = 1.00$, $x_1 = 2 - 1.00 = 1.00$ – correct to $3$ digits.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Small pivot ⇒ large factor ⇒ information is lost in rounding. Pivoting prevents this.

exercises.title: Thomas algorithm 3×3
exercises.description: Solve the tridiagonal system $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&0\\-1&2&-1\\0&-1&2\end{pmatrix}x = \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$ by elimination without pivoting.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
In each column only one entry below the diagonal has to be eliminated.

Step 3: Column 2
$l_{32} = -1/\tfrac32 = -\tfrac23$. $a_{33}' = 2 - (-\tfrac23)(-1) = \tfrac43$; $b_3' = 1 + \tfrac23\cdot\tfrac12 = \tfrac43$.

Step 4: Backward
$x_3 = \tfrac43/\tfrac43 = 1$. $x_2 = (\tfrac12 + 1\cdot 1)/\tfrac32 = 1$. $x_1 = (1 + 1)/2 = 1$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
For tridiagonal matrices one forward sweep and one backward sweep suffice: $O(n)$.

exercises.title: L as a product of elimination matrices
exercises.description: For $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\4&3&3\\8&7&9\end{pmatrix}$ let $G_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\-2&1&0\\-4&0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $G_2 = \begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&-3&1\end{pmatrix}$. Show $G_2G_1A = U$ and $L = G_1^{-1}G_2^{-1}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Each elimination matrix $G_k$ performs one step. The inverses flip the signs.

Step 2: First step
$G_1A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\0&1&1\\0&3&5\end{pmatrix}$ (row 2 $-\,2\cdot$r1, row 3 $-\,4\cdot$r1).

Step 3: Second step
$G_2G_1A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\0&1&1\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix} = U$ (row 3 $-\,3\cdot$r2).

Step 4: Inverse
$G_1^{-1}$ and $G_2^{-1}$ have $+2, +4$ and $+3$. Their product $G_1^{-1}G_2^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\2&1&0\\4&3&1\end{pmatrix} = L$ – the factors sit unchanged in their places.

Step 5: The wrong order
$G_2G_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\-2&1&0\\2&-3&1\end{pmatrix}$: here $+2 = -4 + 6$ stands instead of $-4$. Only the inverses in the order $G_1^{-1}G_2^{-1}$ give the factors cleanly.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
$L$ is so nice because the factors do not mix: that is the magic of the decomposition.

exercises.title: Existence and uniqueness (2×2)
exercises.description: Show: $A = \begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ has an LU decomposition with $l_{ii} = 1$ if and only if $a \neq 0$ (or $c = 0$ already), and the decomposition is unique. State $L$ and $U$ and check $A = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Ansatz $A = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\l&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u_{11}&u_{12}\\0&u_{22}\end{pmatrix}$ and compare coefficients.

Step 2: Comparing coefficients
$\begin{pmatrix}u_{11}&u_{12}\\ l\,u_{11}&l\,u_{12} + u_{22}\end{pmatrix}$: $u_{11} = a$, $u_{12} = b$, $l\,a = c$, $l\,b + u_{22} = d$.

Step 3: Case a ≠ 0
$l = c/a$ is uniquely determined, $u_{22} = d - bc/a = \det A/a$. So exactly one decomposition exists.

Step 4: Case a = 0
Then $l\,a = c$ immediately gives $c = 0$: only if $c = 0$ does every $l$ solve the equation (not unique!); otherwise there is no decomposition. For $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$: $c = 1 \neq 0$ – no LU decomposition.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The 2×2 example shows the condition “leading principal minors $\neq 0$” in miniature; in general: $a_{11}, \det A_{[1:2]},\dots,\det A_{[1:n-1]} \neq 0$.

exercises.title: Uniqueness of the LU decomposition
exercises.description: Let $A$ be invertible and $A = L_1U_1 = L_2U_2$ with unit lower triangular $L_i$ and nonsingular upper triangular $U_i$. Show $L_1 = L_2$, $U_1 = U_2$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Rearrange until a lower triangular matrix stands on the left and an upper triangular one on the right.

Step 2: Rearranging
From $L_1U_1 = L_2U_2$ we get $L_2^{-1}L_1 = U_2U_1^{-1}$. ($L_2$, $U_1$ are invertible because $A$ is.)

Step 3: Structure
Left: product of unit lower triangular matrices – again unit lower triangular. Right: product of upper triangular matrices – upper triangular.

Step 4: Conclusion
A matrix that is both lower and upper triangular with $1$ on the diagonal is the identity: $L_2^{-1}L_1 = I = U_2U_1^{-1}$. Hence $L_1 = L_2$ and $U_1 = U_2$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The normalisation $l_{ii} = 1$ is essential; without it diagonal factors could be shifted between $L$ and $U$.

exercises.title: Deriving the Cholesky formulas
exercises.description: Derive the formulas for $l_{jj}$ and $l_{ij}$ ($i > j$) from $A = LL^T$ and check them on $A = \begin{pmatrix}4&2&2\\2&5&3\\2&3&6\end{pmatrix}$ for the entry $l_{32}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Write out entry $(i,j)$ of $LL^T$: $a_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{\min(i,j)} l_{ik}l_{jk}$.

Step 2: Diagonal
For $i = j$: $a_{jj} = \sum_{k=1}^{j} l_{jk}^2 = \sum_{k<j} l_{jk}^2 + l_{jj}^2$, so $l_{jj} = \sqrt{a_{jj} - \sum_{k<j} l_{jk}^2}$.

Step 3: Below
For $i > j$: $a_{ij} = \sum_{k<j} l_{ik}l_{jk} + l_{ij}\,l_{jj}$, so $l_{ij} = \bigl(a_{ij} - \sum_{k<j} l_{ik}l_{jk}\bigr)/l_{jj}$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The formulas fix the order: column by column from left to right, lower half only.

exercises.title: Positive definiteness via Cholesky
exercises.description: For which $c$ is $A = \begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&c\end{pmatrix}$ positive definite? Decide via Cholesky and test $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Cholesky runs through (all radicands $> 0$) exactly when $A$ is spd.

Step 3: Cross-check
Leading minors: $4 > 0$ and $4c - 4 > 0 \iff c > 1$ – the same result.

Step 4: Second matrix
$\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$: $l_{11} = 1$, $l_{21} = 2$, $l_{22}^2 = 3 - 4 = -1 < 0$. Not positive definite (eigenvalues $2 \pm\sqrt 5$, one negative).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Cholesky is the fastest test for positive definiteness – and delivers the decomposition at the same time.

exercises.title: Cost for tridiagonal matrices
exercises.description: Determine the number of operations of elimination without pivoting for a tridiagonal matrix of size $n$ including solving and compare for $n = 10^6$ with a full matrix.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Only one entry per column has to be eliminated; only two diagonal entries and one right-hand side change.

Step 2: Decomposition
Per step: $1$ division ($l$), $1$ multiplication and $1$ subtraction (new diagonal entry): $3(n-1)$ operations.

Step 3: Solving
Forward: $2(n-1)$ ($1$ mult., $1$ sub.). Backward: $3n$ ($1$ div., $1$ mult., $1$ sub. per row). In total $\approx 8n$.

Step 4: Comparison
$n = 10^6$: $8\cdot 10^6$ flops – milliseconds. Full matrix: $\tfrac23 10^{18} \approx 6.7\cdot 10^{17}$ flops – at $10^{10}$ flops/s about $2$ years; also $8\,\text{TB}$ of memory.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Exploit structure: band matrices save not only time ($O(n)$ instead of $O(n^3)$) but above all memory.

exercises.title: Rank-1 update (Sherman–Morrison)
exercises.description: For invertible $A$ we have $(A + uv^T)^{-1}b = A^{-1}b - \dfrac{A^{-1}u\,(v^TA^{-1}b)}{1 + v^TA^{-1}u}$. Explain why this costs only $O(n^2)$ given an existing LU decomposition of $A$, and check it for $A = 2I$, $u = (1,0)^T$, $v = (0,1)^T$, $b = (3,2)^T$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The formula needs only two solves with $A$ and inner products.

Step 2: Cost
$A^{-1}b$ and $A^{-1}u$ are two solves with the existing decomposition ($2\cdot 2n^2$), each $v^T(\cdot)$ costs $2n$, the rest is $O(n)$. A new decomposition of $A + uv^T$ would cost $\tfrac23 n^3$.

Step 3: Numerical example
$A + uv^T = \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$. $A^{-1}b = (1.5, 1)^T$, $A^{-1}u = (0.5, 0)^T$, $v^TA^{-1}b = 1$, $v^TA^{-1}u = 0$.

Step 4: Result
$x = (1.5, 1)^T - \dfrac{(0.5, 0)^T\cdot 1}{1 + 0} = (1, 1)^T$. Check: $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}(1,1)^T = (3, 2)^T$ ✓.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Small changes of a matrix (rank 1) can be incorporated without a new decomposition – the basis of many update methods (e.g. Broyden, 4.8).

exercises.title: Growth factor in pivoting
exercises.description: Compute $PA = LU$ for $A = \begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\-1&1&1\\-1&-1&1\end{pmatrix}$. How large is $\max|u_{ij}|/\max|a_{ij}|$? Why is growth possible despite $|l_{ik}| \le 1$?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Elimination with partial pivoting; all column maxima equal $1$, so there is no swap.

Step 4: Result
$U = \begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&2\\0&0&4\end{pmatrix}$, $P = I$. Growth factor $4/1 = 4 = 2^{n-1}$.

Step 5: Explanation
The factors are $\le 1$ but each elimination may add magnitudes of a row: the last entry can double at each step. This worst-case growth $2^{n-1}$ practically never occurs in practice.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Partial pivoting is stable in practice, in theory provable only with growth factor $\le 2^{n-1}$.

exercises.title: LU with a parameter
exercises.description: For $A_t = \begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\1&t&1\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}$ determine the LU decomposition without pivoting as a function of $t$. For which $t$ does it exist, for which is $A_t$ nonsingular?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Elimination with a parameter; watch for when a pivot becomes $0$.

Step 3: Step 2
The pivot $t - 1$ must be $\neq 0$. $l_{32} = \dfrac{1}{t-1}$, $u_{33} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{t-1} = \dfrac{t-2}{t-1}$.

Step 4: Existence
The LU decomposition without pivoting exists exactly for $t \neq 1$. For $t = 3$: $l_{32} = \tfrac12$, $u_{33} = \tfrac12$ (matches a direct computation).

Step 5: Nonsingularity
$\det A_t = 1\cdot(t-1)\cdot\dfrac{t-2}{t-1} = t - 2$ for $t \ne 1$; directly: $\det A_t = t - 2$ for all $t$. So nonsingular exactly for $t \neq 2$. For $t = 1$, $A_1$ is nonsingular but not decomposable without a row swap.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Nonsingular ≠ decomposable without pivoting. With a row swap ($PA = LU$) the decomposition exists for every nonsingular matrix.
